# Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Nephrology > Glomerular diseases > Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis*

[Original Article Link](/library/Lg0wD2)

---

## Summary

Poststreptococcal <u>glomerulonephritis</u> (PSGN) is an acute <u>glomerular</u> inflammation that follows infection with nephritogenic strains of <u>streptococci</u>. Although most commonly seen in children following <u>group A streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis</u>, <u>skin infections</u> such as <u>impetigo</u> may also trigger PSGN. Individuals aged > 60 years (especially those with <u>diabetes</u>, <u>malignancy</u>, or <u>alcohol</u> dependency) may also be affected. Deposition of <u>immune complexes</u> within the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u> results in <u>complement</u> activation and subsequent damage to the <u>glomeruli</u>. PSGN typically manifests as <u>nephritic syndrome</u> with <u>hematuria</u>, mild <u>proteinuria</u>, <u>edema</u>, and <u>hypertension</u>. Evidence of recent <u>streptococcal</u> infection (e.g., elevated <u>antistreptolysin O</u> (<u>ASO</u>) and/or <u>anti-DNase B</u> <u>titers</u>) and low <u>complement</u> levels support the diagnosis. Close monitoring and supportive management of <u>edema</u> and <u>hypertension</u> are usually sufficient. <u>Antibiotic therapy</u> is indicated if there is evidence of active <u>GAS infection</u>, primarily to minimize the risk of complications and community spread. While most children recover fully, adults are more likely to develop <u>rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis</u> and/or <u>end-stage kidney disease</u> and may require long-term monitoring.

---

## Epidemiology

* Bimodal age distribution; mostly affects children (between the ages of 3–12 years) and patients > 60 years of age

* The <u>incidence</u> of PSGN has decreased in developed countries due to the systematic use of <u>antibiotics</u> and improved hygienic standards.




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Prior infection with <u>group A beta-hemolytic streptococci</u> (<u>GAS</u>)

* Site of infection

* In children

* Infection of the mouth and <u>pharynx</u> (<u>tonsillitis</u>, <u>pharyngitis</u>): PSGN typically arises 1–3 weeks following infection.

* <u>Soft tissue infections</u> (<u>erysipelas</u>, <u>impetigo</u>): PSGN typically arises 1–6 weeks following infection.

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>

* In adults, the site of infection is usually not the respiratory tract.





> [!TIP]
> Infection-associated <u>glomerulonephritis</u> can also occur following other bacterial infections (e.g., with <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u>, <u>Staphylococcus epidermidis</u>, <u>gram-negative bacteria</u>), viral infections, or <u>malaria</u>, and it can also manifest during an acute infection. [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Infective endocarditis</u> is a common cause of <u>staphylococcus</u> infection-associated <u>glomerulonephritis</u>, especially among individuals who use intravenous drugs. [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)

---

## Pathophysiology

Infection with nephritogenic strains of <u>group A beta-hemolytic streptococci</u> → <u>immune complexes</u> containing the <u>streptococcal</u> <u>antigen</u> deposit within the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u>;  (likely involves <u>molecular mimicry</u>) → <u>complement</u> activation (↑ consumption of <u>complement factors</u>) → destruction of the <u>glomeruli</u> → immune complex-mediated <u>glomerulonephritis</u> and <u>nephritic syndrome</u> (see “<u>Glomerular diseases</u>” for more information)

---

## Clinical features

Approx. 50% of patients remain asymptomatic.;  Symptoms occur approximately 1–6 weeks following an acute infection.




* <u>Nephritic syndrome</u>

* <u>Hematuria</u>: tea- or cola-colored urine

* <u>Hypertension</u>: can lead to <u>headaches</u>

* <u>Edema</u> (prominent facial <u>edema</u>)

* <u>Oliguria</u>

* <u>Influenza</u>-like symptoms

* Flank <u>pain</u>

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[3]](/library/dAcoiU0)




* The <u>diagnosis of PSGN</u> is typically based on confirming a preceding <u>streptococcal</u> infection in an individual with features of acute <u>glomerulonephritis</u>.

* The characteristic findings in PSGN include:

* <u>Nephritic sediment</u> and non-<u>nephrotic range proteinuria</u> on <u>urinalysis</u>

* Evidence of preceding <u>streptococcal</u> infection:

* Elevated antistreptococcal <u>antibody</u> <u>titers</u> (<u>ASO</u>, <u>anti-DNase B antibodies</u>)

* Or, in patients with active infection, positive <u>rapid strep test</u> or cultures

* Low <u>C3 complement</u> with normal C4 <u>complement</u>

* In case of diagnostic uncertainty, consider the following to evaluate for other <u>causes of glomerulonephritis</u>:

* <u>Renal biopsy</u>

* <u>Serology</u> (e.g., <u>factor B</u> <u>antibody</u> levels, anti-<u>GBM</u> <u>antibody</u>, <u>ANA</u>, <u>ANCA</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Suspect PSGN in individuals with features of <u>nephritic syndrome</u> and a recent history of <u>GAS infection</u>. [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)




### Initial evaluation [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)




The following studies are typically routinely obtained in the initial workup for <u>glomerular disease</u>. Findings supportive of PSGN are detailed here. [[3]](/library/dAcoiU0)




* <u>Urinalysis</u> with microscopy: <u>nephritic sediment</u>

* <u>Hematuria</u> with <u>RBC casts</u>

* <u>Proteinuria</u>

* <u>Pyuria</u>

* Quantification of <u>proteinuria</u>: typically shows non-<u>nephrotic range proteinuria</u>  [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)

* <u>Urine protein/creatinine ratio</u>: usually < 300 mg/g  [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)

* <u>24-hour urine collection</u> (less commonly obtained): usually 300–3,400 mg/24 h [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)

* <u>BMP</u> may reveal: [[6]](/library/nf175T0)

* ↑ <u>BUN</u>, ↑ <u>creatinine</u>

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* <u>CBC</u>: : may show <u>normocytic</u>, normochromic <u>anemia</u> [[7]](/library/Jg1swT0)

* <u>C3 complement</u>, C4 <u>complement</u> levels: : classically shows ↓ <u>C3 complement</u> with normal C4 <u>complement</u>   [[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[8]](/library/4i137g0)





### Evidence of preceding <u>GAS infection</u> [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)




* Antistreptococcal <u>antibody</u> <u>titers</u>

* Indication: all patients with suspected PSGN

* Findings: ↑ <u>ASO</u>; , ↑ <u>anti-DNase B antibodies</u>, ↑ antihyaluronidase <u>antibodies</u>

* Isolation of <u>group A beta-hemolytic streptococci</u>

* Indication: suspected active <u>GAS infection</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Pharyngitis</u>: <u>rapid strep test</u>, throat culture

* <u>Skin</u> lesions: wound cultures





> [!TIP]
> PSGN typically occurs following a <u>GAS infection</u> rather than during an active infection. Obtain appropriate diagnostic studies to isolate <u>group A beta-hemolytic streptococci</u> only if active infection is suspected. [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)




![Red blood cell (RBC) casts in urine sediment](media/ua001ixegsnk5vrvnr6ft0hd.jpg)

Red blood cell (RBC) casts in urine sediment




### Additional studies [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)




Consider the following studies in case of diagnostic uncertainty.




* <u>Factor B</u> <u>antibody</u> levels  [[9]](/library/WAcPiU0)[[10]](/library/HN1Kch0)

* <u>Rheumatoid factor</u> and <u>cryoglobulin</u> levels  [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[3]](/library/dAcoiU0)

* <u>ANA</u>, <u>ANCA</u>, anti-<u>GBM</u> <u>antibody</u>  [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)





> [!TIP]
> In patients with decreased <u>C3 complement</u> levels, <u>factor B</u> <u>antibody</u> levels may help distinguish between PSGN (elevated <u>factor B</u> levels) and <u>C3 glomerulopathy</u> (normal <u>factor B</u> levels). A <u>renal biopsy</u> is indicated in individuals with low C3 levels and normal <u>factor B</u> <u>antibody</u> levels to confirm <u>C3 glomerulopathy</u> [[9]](/library/WAcPiU0)[[10]](/library/HN1Kch0)




> [!WARNING]
> If both C3 and C4 <u>complement</u> levels are decreased in a patient with features of <u>glomerulonephritis</u>, consider other causes of immune-complex mediated <u>glomerulonephritis</u>. [[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)




#### <u>Renal ultrasound</u> [[11]](/library/aT1Q6T0)




* Indications: may be obtained during a diagnostic workup of <u>hematuria</u>

* Findings: typically normal; may show nonspecific <u>increased echogenicity</u> of the <u>renal cortex</u>





#### <u>Renal biopsy</u> [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[12]](/library/pAcLkU0)




* Indications: (not routinely performed) 

* Signs of <u>rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis</u>

* Atypical presentation

* Persistently low <u>complement</u> levels > 12 weeks  [[10]](/library/HN1Kch0)

* Persistent <u>proteinuria</u> and <u>hypertension</u> > 1 year [[6]](/library/nf175T0)

* Supportive findings: proliferative glomerulopathy with <u>immune complex</u> deposits  [[13]](/library/KAcUkU0)

* <u>Light microscopy</u>: enlarged and hypercellular <u>glomeruli</u>

* Immunofluorescent microscopy: granular deposits in the <u>glomerular</u> mesangium and <u>capillaries</u> ;  [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[13]](/library/KAcUkU0)

* Consisting of <u>IgG</u>, <u>IgM</u>, <u>C3 complement</u>  [[13]](/library/KAcUkU0)

* Lumpy-bumpy appearance (also called a starry sky appearance)  [[14]](/library/ueYp0o)

* <u>Electron microscopy</u>: <u>immune complexes</u> between the <u>epithelial</u> cell layer and the <u>glomerular basement membrane</u> ; (referred to as subepithelial humps)   [[12]](/library/pAcLkU0)[[13]](/library/KAcUkU0)

## Differential diagnoses

* See “<u>Diseases associated with nephritic syndrome</u>.”

* Glomerulonephritis with low serum complement levels [[15]](/library/5i1iHg0)

* PSGN

* <u>C3 glomerulopathy</u>

* <u>Cryoglobulinemic</u> <u>glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis</u>

* Shunt nephritis

* <u>Infective endocarditis</u>-associated <u>glomerulonephritis</u>

* Glomerulonephritis with normal serum complement levels [[15]](/library/5i1iHg0)

* <u>IgA nephropathy</u>  [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)

* <u>Hemolytic uremic syndrome</u>

* <u>Anti-GBM disease</u>

* <u>Henoch Schonlein purpura</u>




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

Most cases of PSGN are <u>self-limiting</u> and complications of <u>volume overload</u> are managed with supportive treatment.




### General principles [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)




* Consult nephrology to develop a treatment plan.

* Admit patients with any of the following indications of severe disease: [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[6]](/library/nf175T0) 

* <u>Indications for dialysis</u>

* Moderate to severe <u>AKI</u> or progressive <u>renal failure</u>

* <u>Hypertensive crisis</u> (e.g., neurological symptoms of <u>posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome</u>) [[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)

* Manage associated symptoms (e.g., <u>edema</u>, <u>hypertension</u>) as needed.

* Treat current infection, if present.

* Monitor blood pressure, <u>BMP</u>, <u>urinalysis</u>, urine protein, and <u>complement</u> levels until they return to baseline.  [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[4]](/library/kIYm1q)[[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)





> [!WARNING]
> Progressive <u>renal failure</u> suggests <u>rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis</u>; obtain a <u>renal biopsy</u> and initiate treatment promptly to prevent <u>end-stage renal disease</u>. [[5]](/library/Od1IJf0)[[6]](/library/nf175T0)




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)




See also “<u>Supportive care for AKI</u>.”




#### Management of <u>edema</u> and <u>volume overload</u>




* <u>Low-sodium diet</u>: < 2 g/day

* Fluid restriction (e.g., < 2 L per day) [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)

* <u>Loop diuretics</u>   [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[6]](/library/nf175T0)





#### <u>Antihypertensives</u> [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[12]](/library/pAcLkU0)




* Indicated for <u>hypertension</u> refractory to management of <u>edema</u> and <u>volume overload</u>

* Preferred agents include:

* <u>Calcium channel blockers</u> (e.g., <u>nifedipine</u>)

* <u>ACE inhibitors</u> or <u>ARBs</u> 

* Uncertain benefit, given the <u>self-limited</u> nature of PSGN [[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[6]](/library/nf175T0)

* Avoid in patients with rapidly progressive renal dysfunction.

* Consider in patients with concomitant <u>proteinuria</u>, unless there are <u>contraindications for ACE inhibitors and ARBs</u>. [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)

* Requires close <u>BMP</u> monitoring for progressive <u>AKI</u> and <u>hyperkalemia</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>ACE inhibitors</u> and <u>ARBs</u> in patients with rapidly worsening renal function and/or sudden onset of <u>nephrotic range proteinuria</u>, as these medications can exacerbate <u>AKI</u> and <u>hyperkalemia</u>. [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)




### <u>Antibiotic therapy</u>




<u>Antibiotics</u> do not affect the course of PSGN but should be administered in individuals with active <u>GAS infection</u> to prevent complications (e.g., <u>abscess</u>, <u>rheumatic fever</u>) and community <u>outbreak</u> of nephritogenic strains of <u>S. pyogenes</u>. [[16]](/library/wychhU0)




* Indication: evidence of active infection (e.g., positive cultures for <u>GAS</u>) to prevent [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)

* Regimens: should be based on the site of infection; follow local protocols when available.

* <u>GAS tonsillopharyngitis</u>: Initiate <u>recommended antibiotic regimens for acute GAS pharyngitis</u>.

* <u>Skin and soft tissue infections</u> (e.g., <u>impetigo</u>): Begin <u>empiric antibiotic therapy for skin and soft tissue infections</u>.





### Role of <u>glucocorticoids</u> [[1]](/library/Dyc1hU0)[[2]](/library/qAcCkU0)[[12]](/library/pAcLkU0)




* <u>Glucocorticoids</u> are not routinely indicated for PSGN (unproven benefit).

* High-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u> may be considered in combination with other <u>immunosuppressants</u> for patients with severe disease.

---

## Complications

Complications are more common in adults:




* <u>Acute renal failure</u>

* <u>Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis</u>

* <u>Nephrotic syndrome</u> later in the course of the disease





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.

---

## Prognosis

* Recovery usually occurs within 6–8 weeks.

* In children: restitution of <u>kidney function</u> in > 90% of cases

* In some cases, <u>urinalysis</u> may remain abnormal for extended periods.

* In adults, about 50% of patients suffer from persistently reduced renal function.

---
